text: Figure 4 supports a task-specific reward-time trade-off rather than unlimited scaling. To prevent curriculum-driven difficulty changes from confounding reward, the experiment reduces maximum stair and obstacle heights and trains without the curriculum. It reports total episode reward as mean and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, more robots mean fewer consecutive steps per robot: training time decreases, but reward drops sharply at excessive parallelism, consistent with inadequate temporal information for advantage estimation. Throughput gains also slow beyond roughly 4,000 robots. With fewer robots, reward declines more gradually; the authors suggest this reflects less diverse, correlated samples from longer trajectories. Larger batches yield higher reward and delay the high-parallelism drop, while increasing training time. The 20,000-robot baseline uses 50 steps per robot and one million samples per update; it achieves the highest reward at greater training cost, not under a matched sample budget. Thus, about 2,048-4,096 robots with approximately 100,000-200,000 samples per batch balance reward and time for this simplified task, subject to temporal-data requirements and throughput saturation.

Rapid terrain-aware locomotion training must accelerate experience collection without sacrificing coherent trajectories. Keeping simulation, data collection, and proximal policy optimization (PPO) on one GPU reduces CPU-GPU transfers. Because the shared mesh cannot readily change at resets, an adaptive curriculum relocates robots among tiled terrains, advancing successful robots and lowering difficulty after insufficient progress without regenerating terrain. Large minibatches and time-out bootstrapping adapt PPO to this setting, but adequate per-robot rollout lengths constrain useful parallelism. The policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights; friction randomization, observation noise, pushes, and actuator modeling prepare it for transfer. With 4,096 ANYmal C robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 updates, training took under 20 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation. In simulation, stair crossings without base contact achieved nearly 100% success for steps up to 0.2 m, but obstacle success declined with difficulty and uphill traversal failed beyond 25 degrees. The fixed policy negotiated stairs and obstacles on physical ANYmal C, establishing hardware deployment under this setup, although imperfect lidar-derived terrain maps reduced robustness and prompted limiting velocity commands to 0.6 m/s.

PPO's critic predicts an infinite-horizon discounted return, but a reset does not always mean that future return is zero. Failure or goal completion ends the task trajectory and can be anticipated by the critic; a time limit instead interrupts a continuing trajectory. Because episode time is absent from observations, the critic cannot anticipate that interruption. Treating it as terminal would remove continuation value for a reason unavailable to the critic. The environment therefore distinguishes time-outs and augments their rewards with the critic's discounted prediction of future return, bootstrapping the target for the interrupted trajectory rather than the episode begun after reset. This distinction remains necessary with short rollouts: the 20-second episode limit is independent of the number of steps collected per policy update, and environments are not reset after every update. Episodes can consequently span multiple batches, so time-outs cannot be assumed absent or restricted to the final collection step.

Rapid training of terrain-aware locomotion requires both high simulation throughput and trajectories that remain informative for learning. Keeping Isaac Gym simulation, policy inference, observations, rewards, and proximal policy optimization on one GPU reduces CPU-GPU transfers. A performance-adaptive curriculum raises difficulty after successful traversal and lowers it after insufficient progress by relocating robots among prebuilt terrain tiles, avoiding regeneration. A single policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights to follow motion commands. With 4,096 robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 policy updates, an ANYmal C policy trains in under 20 minutes on an i9-11900k/RTX A6000 workstation. This speed depends on retaining adequate consecutive rollout steps per robot: increasing parallelism at fixed batch size eventually shortens trajectories enough to impair learning. Simulation tests show nearly complete traversal success without base contact on stairs up to 0.2 m, declining success on randomized obstacles, and failed climbing beyond 25-degree slopes. The fixed policy also negotiates stairs and obstacles on hardware, but imperfect elevation maps reduce robustness, prompting a 0.6 m/s command limit. Together, these results establish rapid training and physical deployment under the reported configuration, bounded by rollout duration and terrain sensing.

Figure 4 shows that faster collection does not necessarily produce a better policy. On a simplified task without the curriculum and with reduced stair and obstacle difficulty, it compares mean episode reward and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, increasing robot count reduces training time but shortens each robot's rollout. Reward drops sharply at excessive counts, which the authors explain by inadequate temporal information for generalized advantage estimation. Conversely, they hypothesize that the gradual reward decline at small counts reflects less diverse samples from longer individual trajectories. Throughput scales nearly linearly up to about 4,000 robots before gains slow. Larger batches improve reward and permit more robots before deterioration, but take longer to train; the 20,000-robot, million-sample baseline attains the highest reward at a longer training duration. Thus, about 2,048-4,096 robots with roughly 100,000-200,000 samples per batch balance reward and training time for this task, rather than supporting unlimited parallelism.

Proximal policy optimization (PPO) uses a critic to estimate an infinite-horizon sum of discounted future rewards, but resets can truncate that return. Failures and goal completion are predictable task endings. Time limits are different: episode time is absent from observations, so the critic cannot anticipate when an otherwise continuing trajectory will be interrupted. Treating that interruption as terminal would discard its predicted future return. The modified environment interface therefore reports time-outs separately, and the reward at a time-out is augmented with the critic's discounted estimate of the remaining return. The critic target thus includes continuation value rather than treating the reset as task completion. Episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short rollout batches, so time-outs can occur within a batch, not just at its final step. A policy update does not itself reset the environments.
